papers.title: Mouse bio-behavioral phenotyping using a digital homecage framework for long-timescale, high-resolution, and multi-factor data collection and analytics.
papers.abstract: Long-term monitoring of behavioral and physiological processes is essential for elucidating complex brain-based phenomena and disorders that develop over extended periods, such as chronic stress, circadian disruption, and metabolic syndromes. Though digital phenotyping is well-established in humans via smart devices, comparable solutions for rodent models remain limited. To address this gap, we present the Digital Homecage (DHC) system, an open-source platform that enables uninterrupted, long-timescale recording of over 20 behavioral metrics in single-housed mice. The DHC integrates video capture, operant task modules, and wheel-running data to achieve sub-second resolution in monitoring behaviors such as actigraphy, sleep, grooming, and food choice over periods spanning weeks. Initial data validate the system's capability to reveal circadian patterns across multiple spontaneous behaviors, consistently reflecting nocturnal activity. The DHC offers unique opportunities for longitudinal analyses of chronic conditions and neuropsychiatric syndromes. Its accessibility and modular design promote community-driven innovation, establishing the DHC as a transformative tool for advancing the study of complex traits in rodent models of brain function and behavior. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-69041-0.

papers.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
papers.abstract: Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.

papers.title: Optogenetics in neurobiology and neurodegenerative disorders: from neural circuit mechanisms to precision neuromodulation.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis and stroke, are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment and neural circuit degeneration, leading to severe cognitive and motor deficits. Although considerable progress has been made in understanding their molecular pathology, the circuit level mechanisms driving disease onset and progression remain incompletely understood. Optogenetics, which combines microbial opsins, genetic engineering and optical stimulation, enables reversible, cell-specific control of neuronal activity with millisecond precision and has transformed neuroscience from observational analysis to causal investigation of neural circuits. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular basis of optogenetics, microbial opsins, gene delivery strategies and optical stimulation technologies, together with their applications in basic neurobiology and neurodegenerative disease research. We discuss how optogenetics has advanced understanding of neural circuit organization, synaptic plasticity, memory, neurodevelopment, sleep regulation, protein aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress and regulated cell death. Although these studies have generated important mechanistic insights and demonstrated functional improvements in experimental models, translation into human therapies remains investigational due to challenges associated with gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune compatibility and optical accessibility. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including closed-loop neuromodulation, wireless photostimulation, artificial intelligence-assisted neural decoding, nanotechnology enabled light delivery and brain computer interfaces, are critically evaluated with emphasis on their current evidence status, translational challenges and limitations for clinical implementation. Collectively, optogenetics provides an unprecedented platform for deciphering disease mechanisms and evaluating circuit-based neuromodulation strategies, while continued technological and biological validation will determine its future role in precision therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background. Despite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. Methods. We pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohen's d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. Results. Three features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. Conclusions. This study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.

papers.title: Regional cingulate metabolite-ratio differences exceed longitudinal changes across an approximately 34-h protocol: a prospective quality-controlled proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy study.
papers.abstract: Regional organization, acquisition sequence, and measurement quality can obscure the interpretation of longitudinal proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) changes. We compared anterior vs. posterior cingulate metabolite-ratio differences with changes across an approximately 34-h protocol and tested whether findings depended on sequence, quality-control rules, respiratory burden, comorbidity, or polysomnographic sleep measures. In this prospective single-center observational study, 138 university-affiliated and advertisement-recruited participants underwent baseline evening spectroscopy of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) on day 1, full-night polysomnography from day 2 into day 3, and post-PSG morning spectroscopy on day 3 using MEGA-PRESS and SVS-PRESS. Among 116 participants with complete paired timestamps, the median interval between scan starts was 34.01 h (IQR, 33.86-34.10 h). Primary metabolite-to-creatine ratios were analyzed using age-, sex-, and body mass index-adjusted generalized estimating equations. Sensitivity analyses evaluated effect magnitude, sequence dependence, spectral-quality selection, follow-up availability, exclusion of participants with apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) ≥15 events/h, exclusion of hypertension or diabetes, and associations between metabolite change and seven polysomnographic measures. A total of 137 participants contributed to adjusted primary models. PCC showed higher NAA/Cr in both sequences and higher SVS GlxT/Cr, whereas ACC showed higher Cho/Cr in both sequences and higher MEGA Glu/Cr (all q < 0.001); PCC also showed higher MEGA GABA/Cr (q = 0.020). Cr2 denotes the vendor-fitted second creatine/phosphocreatine resonance, and GlxT denotes the sum of six vendor-fitted glutamate/glutamine components. Follow-up reductions that survived false-discovery-rate correction were confined to SVS Cr2/Cr and GlxT/Cr. Across 11 outcomes, the median absolute paired standardized effect size was 0.571 for region and 0.125 for longitudinal change; the former was 4.6 times the latter, a ratio of median standardized effect magnitudes rather than a biological fold difference. Excluding AHI ≥ 15 events/h preserved the direction of all 12 primary FDR-significant effects, with 11 remaining q < 0.05. None of 77 polysomnographic dose-response tests survived global correction. In this heterogeneous cohort, regional differences in cingulate metabolite ratios were larger and more robust than longitudinal changes. Because the approximately 34-h contrast combined elapsed time, circadian phase, an intervening monitored night, repositioning, and other uncontrolled influences, it should not be interpreted as a sleep-specific effect. The ratio-based findings should not be interpreted as regional concentration differences.

papers.title: Light-induced melatonin suppression in school-aged children before and during camping: associations with circadian phase and daytime light exposure
papers.abstract: Prior light exposure can influence the magnitude of melatonin suppression in response to evening light, even within the same individual. We examined whether light-induced melatonin suppression in school-aged children differed before and during a camp with approximately two weeks of exposure to a natural light-dark cycle. We also explored interindividual variation in melatonin suppression and its associations with circadian phase, habitual sleep timing, and daytime light exposure. Twenty-one healthy children aged 9--14 years underwent evening light experiments at the start of camp (Pre-camp session) and approximately two weeks later (Camp session). Melatonin suppression was calculated by comparing the area under the melatonin concentration curve between the evening light condition (200 {+/-} 30 lx, 5000 K) and the dim light condition (< 30 lx, incandescent lamps), with integration starting at dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). We assessed sleep habits from 14-day sleep diaries before camping and measured wrist-level illuminance during camping. We examined associations using Spearman correlations and compared Pre-camp and Camp melatonin suppression using a paired t-test. Melatonin suppression did not differ significantly between Pre-camp and Camp sessions (p = 0.21). Greater suppression in the Pre-camp session was associated with later DLMO (rho = 0.49, p = 0.028), but not with habitual sleep variables. In the Camp session, higher same-day geometric mean illuminance was associated with lower suppression (n = 15; rho = -0.58, p = 0.024), whereas 7-day light-exposure metrics were not. Mean melatonin suppression did not significantly change across the camping period. Meanwhile, children showed large interindividual variation in melatonin suppression, and circadian phase and recent daytime light exposure are candidate correlates of this variation in the responsiveness to the evening light.

papers.title: Altered heart-brain coupling in awake patients with isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder.
papers.abstract: Isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) represents a prodromal stage of alpha-synucleinopathies, frequently preceding Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Beyond the characteristic sleep disturbances, alterations in brain-body coupling, reflecting neural peripheral physiological interactions, have yet to be determined. Using whole-night polysomnography, we quantified brain-body coupling via heartbeat evoked potentials (HEPs) across wakefulness, NREM, and REM sleep. Individuals with iRBD (n = 13) were compared with healthy controls (n = 23), alongside analyses of ECG-derived features. During wakefulness, iRBD patients showed altered HEPs over frontal regions between 305 and 445 ms after the R-peak. No significant group differences were observed during NREM or REM sleep, and HEP amplitude alterations were not explained by ECG differences. These diurnal HEP changes may represent a novel quantitative biomarker for iRBD during wakefulness and, in the future, could serve as a marker for phenoconversion to alpha-synucleinopathy.

papers.title: Chronic buprenorphine-associated severe central sleep apnea and desaturation proof of concept.
papers.abstract: Individuals on opioids are found dead in bed and respiratory depression is a potential cause. In contrast to other opioids, buprenorphine, a partial μ-opioid receptor agonist has reduced respiratory depression. However, death has also been reported in individuals using buprenorphine; yet, it is not known if chronic use of buprenorphine could be associated with clinically significant respiratory depression. The purpose of this preliminary study was to determine if chronic buprenorphine use is associated with sleep disordered breathing. A retrospective study of 11 consecutive patients who were using buprenorphine chronically and referred for sleep evaluation. All underwent full night attended polysomnography and polysomnograms were scored page by page by a board-certified sleep physician. Two breathing patterns were observed. First, four patients had central sleep apnea (CSA) with an index of ≥5/h of sleep and an average of 13. When compared to those without CSA, patients with CSA suffered from severe sleep apnea with an apnea hypopnea index (AHI) of 35 (vs.9/hour of sleep) and associated with clinically significant low saturation (75% vs. 87%). Second, the group without significant CSA (CAI <5, n = 7), despite a low AHI, had relatively more sustained desaturation time below 90% (91 vs 51 min), suggesting hypoventilation. Despite improved respiratory safety profile, this preliminary study is the first to provide evidence that chronic use of buprenorphine is associated with clinically significant sleep disorders with two distinct patterns shared with other opioids. These disordered breathing events could be a potential cause of buprenorphine-associated death reported in the literature, a finding also shared with other opioids. Clinicians should be aware of this association.

It provides preliminary evidence that chronic buprenorphine is associated with clinically significant sleep-disordered breathing.

papers.title: Resting-state EEG spectral characteristics before and after a single auditory integration training session in children with autism spectrum disorder.
papers.abstract: Resting-state EEG characteristics may differ between autistic and non-autistic children. Conventional band power mixes periodic and broadband activity; spectral parameterization separates periodic peaks from the aperiodic background. Auditory integration training (AIT) is used as a complementary intervention, but its immediate neurophysiological and clinical effects remain uncertain. We examined baseline EEG differences and pre-post changes around one AIT session. Twenty children with ASD and 15 typically developing (TD) children aged 6-8 years participated. Resting EEG was recorded in ASD before and immediately after a 30-min Berard AIT session. Sixteen ASD participants had usable paired recordings. Relative power was measured in five bands. Periodic and aperiodic components were parameterized with FOOOF. Sensitivity analyses varied R-squared threshold, aperiodic mode, fitting settings, channel aggregation. At baseline, ASD showed higher delta and lower theta, alpha, and beta relative power than TD. After modeling peaks, aperiodic exponent and offset did not differ between groups. Among 16 paired ASD recordings, delta decreased and beta/gamma increased post-session; paired tests of exponent and offset were nonsignificant. Five of 20 baseline and seven of 18 post-session recordings had R-squared<0.90, but sensitivity analyses did not change null aperiodic findings. This uncontrolled pilot study found immediate pre-post band-power differences around one Berard AIT session but no significant FOOOF-derived aperiodic changes. Findings are hypothesis-generating and cannot distinguish AIT-specific effects from repeated measurement, arousal, expectancy, or generic auditory stimulation. Variable fit quality and small sample limit precision; controlled longitudinal studies are needed.

papers.title: Integrating wavelet signal processing and machine learning for EEG-based detection of brain diseases with representative channel selection.
papers.abstract: BackgroundBrain diseases pose a significant global health challenge, and their diagnosis often relies on subjective clinical assessments.ObjectiveTo this end, this study proposes an integrated wavelet signal processing and machine learning framework for single-channel Electroencephalography (EEG)-based detection of brain diseases with representative channel selection.MethodsFirst, EEG signals are decomposed into rhythm-specific sub-bands using the Discrete Wavelet Packet Transform (DWPT). Then, for each rhythm, a multi-dimensional feature matrix (MFM) is constructed by integrating Approximate Entropy (AE), Rhythm Energy Ratio (RER), C0-complexity (C0), and Zero-crossing Rate (ZCR), which comprehensively models the EEG characteristics. Six classifiers were compared under subject-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, and Decision Tree (DT) was selected as the representative classifier. Each channel was then evaluated independently as a complete single-channel system, and representative channels were identified from the completed results.ResultsValidated on publicly available datasets for SCHIZ (schizophrenia), UNM (Parkinson's disease), and MPHCE (depression), the method achieves impressive accuracies of 84.52% (F4), 86.54% (F4), and 93.10% (Fp1), respectively, using single-channel EEG electrode.ConclusionsSuch results demonstrate that the proposed approach maintains robust detection performance in each of the three disease-specific tasks. The framework is lightweight by design, using only a single EEG channel and a single simple machine-learning model for classification. It needs no multi-channel feature concatenation or decision-level fusion. This single-channel design suits hardware and data sources with limited resources, and may support the development of low-cost portable EEG systems.

papers.title: Sub-Threshold Stochastic Vibration Improves Fingertip Tactile Sensitivity in Stroke Survivors and Healthy Adults, with Source-Localized EEG Evidence for Cortical Network Reorganization in Healthy Adults
papers.abstract: Cutaneous sensation is vital for daily function and safety, yet it commonly declines with ageing and after neurological injury, with stroke survivors particularly affected. This study investigates whether sub-threshold stochastic (random) vibrations can enhance light-touch (cutaneous) sensation in healthy adults and stroke survivors and characterizes the associated changes in cortical functional connectivity (FC). Nineteen healthy participants and five stroke survivors took part. A custom device delivered sinusoidal and stochastic vibrations to the volar surface of the right middle fingertip. For each participant we first determined the detection threshold for stochastic vibration alone, then the threshold for a 30 Hz sinusoidal vibration, and then the threshold for that sinusoidal vibration combined with imperceptible stochastic noise fixed at 80% of the stochastic threshold; in ten healthy participants a super-threshold combination (120% of the stochastic threshold) was also tested. High-density (64-channel) electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded throughout for the healthy participants. Adding sub- threshold stochastic noise lowered the sinusoidal detection threshold in every participant tested and produced consistent reductions in all five stroke survivors; expressed as gains in sensitivity, individual improvements reached up to 19 times in healthy participants and up to 4 times in stroke survivors. Source- localized EEG showed that sub-threshold stochastic vibration significantly increased FC, most extensively in the alpha band, with prominent involvement of frontal regions (superior and rostral middle frontal cortices and anterior cingulate; cluster- based permutation p < 0.05), consistent with a noise-driven modulation of sensory and attentional networks. Super-threshold noise produced weaker, predominantly beta-band changes, in line with signal masking rather than resonance. These findings indicate that sub-threshold stochastic vibration lowers light-touch detection thresholds and reorganizes cortical connectivity in both healthy and stroke populations, and they support prioritizing cutaneous sensation in stochastic-resonance based neurorehabilitation for stroke survivors.

papers.title: Robust Feature Engineering Techniques for Designing Efficient Motor Imagery-Based Systems Using Multidomain Electroencephalography
papers.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have potential applications in neurorehabilitation; however, the high dimensionality and complexity of electroencephalography (EEG) signals present challenges for accurate classification. This study aimed to improve the classification of motor and motor imagery activities using multidomain feature engineering and feature selection on the MILimbEEG dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, and wavelet-based features were extracted from 16-channel EEG signals, yielding 416 features. Maximum relevance minimum redundancy (MRMR) was then applied to select the four most informative and minimally redundant features. These features were used to train support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Naive Bayes, and decision tree classifiers, with performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation based on testing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The Gaussian-kernel SVM achieved the highest testing accuracies of 92.50% for motor activities and 95.48% for motor imagery activities. For the highest-performing motor imagery classification, precision, recall, and F1-score were 86.97%, 88.33%, and 87.04%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that reducing 416 multidomain EEG features to four discriminative features using MRMR can maintain strong classification performance. The proposed feature-engineering framework may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based BCI systems for neurorehabilitation applications.

papers.title: Effects of heart rate variability biofeedback and relaxation training on ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity in young patients with depressive disorders: An EEG study.
papers.abstract: Heart rate variability biofeedback (HRVB) may enhance cardiac autonomic regulation and modulate emotion-related brain regions, including the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC). This study compared the effects of HRVB and relaxation training (RT) on electroencephalography (EEG) current source density (CSD) in the bilateral vmPFC of young patients with depressive disorder. Fifty-nine patients were assigned to the HRVB (n = 30) or RT (n = 29) groups and received 60-min sessions twice weekly for five weeks. The HRVB group underwent resonance-frequency breathing with heart rate variability feedback, whereas the RT group underwent relaxation training with heart-rate feedback. After exclusions due to arrhythmia, drop-out, or EEG-related issues, 45 patients were included in the final analysis (HRVB, n = 22; RT, n = 23). Eyes-closed EEG was recorded during pre test rest, post-test rest, and post-test transfer stages. Group × Time effects on bilateral vmPFC CSD were examined across six frequency bands. Compared with the RT group, the HRVB group exhibited greater right vmPFC beta3 CSD and left vmPFC high-beta CSD during the transfer stage. Both groups exhibited increased theta CSD across the stages, indicating shared relaxation effects. HRVB may engage vmPFC-related regulatory processes beyond the relaxation effect observed in RT.

papers.title: Disrupted activation of dot perspective task-related EEG generators in forensic patients with borderline personality disorder.
papers.abstract: Altercentric and egocentric biases (AB, EB) refer to the impact of another agent's/own perspective on the speed with which one can report one's own/another visual perspective respectively. These biases are known to be affected by illnesses and in particular borderline personality (BPD). Coupling the dot-perspective taking task with high-density EEG recordings at the surface and in the inverse space, we analyzed the regional distribution of neural generators related to AB and EB in healthy controls (n = 24) and forensic BPD male patients (n = 14) making comparisons with previous functional MRI data obtained with the same experimental design. In both controls and BPD cases, AB was associated with early EEG activations of visual association areas. In contrast, EB was related to increased use of neural sources in salience, mentalizing networks and mirror neuron areas bilaterally. In forensic BPD patients, no statistically significant differential activation of neural generators was observed in respect to this variable. Our preliminary findings in a small sample of BPD patients show that unlike fMRI observations that pointed to an AB-related widespread increase of BOLD signal in central executive and mentalizing areas, this was not the case at the level of neural generators. Paralleling previous fMRI data, EB was related to increased need of activation of neural sources in visual association areas and later on in several networks involved in social cognition. Such activation was not observed in forensic BPD cases supporting the hypothesis of a decreased ability of these patients in mobilizing their brain resources when treating the Self-Other discrepancy. However, the limited statistical power and post-hoc group-level interaction analysis point to the need for further confirmatory analyses of these first experimental evidences. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-64677-4.

papers.title: Prevalence and Association of Undiagnosed Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Perioperative Neurocognitive Disorders, and Quality of Life After Brain Surgery.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is increasingly seen in neurosurgical patients and can impact patient outcomes. There is a paucity of literature regarding the OSA burden in the neurosurgical population and its link with perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) and quality of life (QoL). Our primary objective was to evaluate the OSA prevalence in patients undergoing brain surgery and, secondarily, to assess its association with postoperative complications of emergence delirium (ED), postoperative delirium (POD), and delayed neurocognitive recovery, sleep, respiratory events, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, hospital stay, 28-day QoL, and functional recovery. This secondary analysis of a primary study was conducted among adults undergoing elective brain surgery over a 14-month period. Patients were screened preoperatively for undiagnosed OSA using the STOP-BANG questionnaire. ED was evaluated using the Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale, POD using the Confusion Assessment Method and PND using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Sleep, Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE) scores and QoL were also assessed. The prevalence of OSA was 31.5% (117/371). OSA was not associated with PND, except at baseline (P = 0.039). Similarly, OSA was not associated with sleep disturbances, respiratory complications, or ICU admission. Higher STOP-BANG scores correlated with longer hospital stays (P = 0.042), lower GOSE scores (P = 0.006), and worse cumulative QoL scores (P = 0.018). Approximately one-third of patients undergoing brain surgery had undiagnosed OSA. Higher STOP-BANG scores were associated with preoperative cognitive impairment. Although OSA was not associated with sleep disturbances or PND, higher STOP-BANG scores were associated with unfavorable functional recovery and poorer QoL 28 days after surgery.

papers.title: Cortical Network Alterations and Treatment-Induced Reorganization in Panic Disorder: A Longitudinal High-Density EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Although neuroimaging has identified network abnormalities in panic disorder (PD), the rapid and transient nature of panic symptoms highlights the need for methods with high temporal resolution. This study used high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate cortical network alterations in PD and explore their potential as translational biomarkers. This longitudinal study enrolled 52 drug-naïve PD patients and 43 healthy controls. High-density (128-channel) resting-state EEG was collected from both groups at baseline, with repeat assessments performed in PD patients after 6 weeks of venlafaxine treatment. Source-level functional connectivity and network topology were analyzed to characterize cortical network features. Support vector machine (SVM) was used to evaluate the discriminative potential of baseline network features. At baseline, PD patients showed frequency-specific network disruptions, with enhanced connectivity within and between the default mode network, frontoparietal network, and dorsal attention network in the α band, but reduced connectivity across multiple networks in the θ and δ bands. Graph theory analysis revealed decreased global efficiency and increased characteristic path length in the α and δ bands. The SVM classifier achieved 86.32% accuracy in distinguishing PD patients from controls. Following treatment, clinical improvement was accompanied by network reorganization, including increased global efficiency and small-worldness in the α band, and enhanced fronto-temporal connectivity in the δ band. Exploratory brain-behavior associations did not survive FDR correction. PD is characterized by frequency-specific cortical network disruptions that show dynamic reorganization following treatment. These findings highlight the potential of EEG-derived network features as candidate markers for PD identification and treatment monitoring.

papers.title: Who gets enough sleep? - Sleep duration and classification based on sleep recommendations among the adult population in Germany.
papers.abstract: An insufficient or excessive sleep duration can be associated with various health risks. The National Sleep Foundation recommends seven to nine hours' sleep per night for 18 - 64-year-olds and seven to eight hours' sleep for adults aged 65 and older. The aim of this study is to describe the sleep duration in the adult population in Germany and to identify population groups that meet the sleep duration recommendations. Using data from the GEDA 2023 telephone survey, the mean sleep duration and the prevalence of adherence to sleep recommendations were calculated for weekdays, weekends and the whole week, stratified by gender, age group and educational group. In addition, bedtimes were grouped into categories and predicted probabilities of meeting the recommendations were estimated. On average, the adult population in Germany sleeps for 07:26 hours per night, with longer sleep duration at the weekend, particularly among 18 - 29-year-olds (07:20 hours vs. 08:23 hours). On average, women sleep longer than men (07:31 hours vs. 07:20 hours). Overall, 51.6 % meet the recommended sleep duration, more frequently at weekends than on weekdays (54.7 % vs. 46.7 %) and among those with higher level of education (62.5 %). Later bedtimes are associated with a lower likelihood of meeting the recommendations. Continuous monitoring of sleep behaviour should be established as part of national health monitoring. Additional sleep parameters, such as sleep quality and sleep disorders, should also be taken into account to identify at-risk groups and to target public health measures effectively.

papers.title: Sleep and circadian disturbances in Alzheimer's disease: clinical assessment, treatable syndromes, and limits of biomarker inference.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian disturbances in Alzheimer's disease (AD) affect patients and caregivers, but clinical action depends on the syndrome, measurement, and outcome under consideration. This narrative review links sleep assessment to indication-based care while distinguishing symptomatic benefit, physiological target engagement, and disease modification. A purposive literature search was supplemented by targeted checks of PubMed-indexed and original publisher records through 4 October 2026. Selected studies are described by population, AD ascertainment, comparator, and measured endpoint rather than assigned formal evidence-certainty grades. Actigraphy characterizes behavioral rest-activity patterns; melatonin timing and temperature rhythms address endogenous circadian physiology under controlled conditions. Polysomnography and quantitative electroencephalography characterize respiratory events, sleep architecture, and oscillatory activity. These measurements inform different questions and do not independently assign AD etiology or cognitive-functional stage. Clinical priorities include confirmed obstructive sleep apnea, cognition-adapted insomnia care, irregular sleep timing, medication-related effects, parasomnias, limb symptoms, and excessive daytime sleepiness. Interpretation incorporates hypoxemia, treatment exposure, comorbidity, caregiver support, and competing diagnoses. Randomized sleep benefits remain distinct from observational cognitive associations or exploratory imaging and cerebrospinal fluid changes. Human and animal studies of arousal circuits, protein dynamics, inflammation, and fluid transport provide mechanistic context, with conflicting results interpreted according to the actual experimental endpoint. The review provides a clinically organized account of selected evidence, not a comprehensive treatment ranking. Sleep care and cognitive-etiologic assessment should proceed in parallel, with follow-up matched to patient function, safety, and the specific treatment goal.

papers.title: Comparative EEG analysis of Sutra and Tantra meditations: insights into meditative states and long-term traits.
papers.abstract: The Tibetan Buddhist tradition distinguishes between two broad categories of meditation: Sutra and Tantra, which differ in the methods and mental faculties they employ. The main neurophysiological studies of Tibetan Buddhist meditation have been conducted mostly on Sutra practices; while Tantric meditation remains less studied. This publication presents a dual comparative study, using both between-groups and within-subjects design, of the neurophysiological (EEG) correlates characterizing Sutra and Tantra meditative practices, examining both the meditative states and the meditative traits. The study was carried out within the natural environment of Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in India, maintaining the socio-cultural context. Two groups of long-term practitioners (Buddhist monks of Gelug lineage), one experienced in the Tantra tradition (T-group, n = 21) and the other in the Sutra tradition (S-group, n = 20) participated in the study. A between-group cluster permutation test revealed that the groups differed in EEG alpha power during meditation, as well as in baseline resting conditions before and after meditation. Specifically, T-group demonstrated consistently lower alpha power compared to the S-group, regardless of the conditions. Thus, the observed differences are stable characteristics of the groups. The within-subjects analysis demonstrated that the conditions (meditation, and baseline resting states before and after meditation) differed only in the T-group: during meditation, an increase in individual alpha peak frequency (iAPF) was observed in the occipital leads, followed by a decrease in iAPF after meditation. We suggest that reported between-group differences represent enduring meditative traits developed through years of training in meditative techniques in the Sutra and Tantra traditions. Nevertheless, we cannot entirely exclude the possibility that these variations may also stem from certain cohort-specific characteristics unrelated to meditation. An examination of individual power spectra revealed that the absence of significant differences in EEG spectral power between conditions can be primarily attributed to the inter-individual variability in both groups. This variability, in turn, may stem from extensive expertise of highly experienced practitioners, who over years of training, develop individualized cognitive strategies for maintaining the meditative state. Our future research will focus on a more detailed quantitative analysis of inter-individual variability during meditations and on identifying additional between-group differences among practitioners in different traditions.

papers.title: Association of Self-Reported Sleep and Circadian Variability and Moral Judgements and Decision-Making.
papers.abstract: Sleep and social processes are bidirectionally interrelated. Circadian factors such as sleep duration, quality, and chronotype can influence social processing, including moral judgements and decision-making. We investigated the associations of self-reported sleep and circadian factors with measures of human moral and social judgements, including online vigilantism, aversion to causing and witnessing harm, and generosity. A total of 109 healthy adults (18-39 years) completed an observational online survey of self-report measures of sleep and circadian factors (quality, chronotype, sleep regularity, social jetlag), as well as self-report or behavioural measures related to moral concerns, such as willingness to engage in online vigilantism, aversion to causing and witnessing harm to others, and generosity (the Dictator Game). We found significant associations between increased online vigilantism and earlier chronotype, higher sleep regularity, and less social jetlag (r > 0.20, all p < 0.05), and between aversion to causing and witnessing harm and sleep regularity (r > 0.20, all p < 0.05), but not for dictator game generosity (p > 0.06). Hierarchical regression analyses identified moderate effect sizes for sleep regularity and (to a lesser extent) social jetlag as significant contributors to vigilantism and aversion to causing and witnessing harm (R2 > 0.21, all p < 0.05), after controlling for sociodemographic characteristics, mental health conditions, and medication intake. A small, non-significant effect size was identified for sleep quality and dictator game generosity (R2 = 0.13, p = 0.06). The findings highlight the importance of considering sleep and circadian regularity in human moral judgements and decision-making.

papers.title: Quantitative effects of sleep deprivation on digital pupillary dynamics and visual evoked potential metrics in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: The pupillary light reflex (PLR), pupillary sleepiness test (PST), and visual evoked potentials (VEPs) are crucial for assessing the functional integrity of the visual and autonomic nervous systems. These responses integrate retinal phototransduction with midbrain reflex pathways and cortical visual processing, all of which are influenced by physiological and clinical disorders. Their temporal dynamics lay the groundwork for using pupillary reflexes and cortical potentials as biomarkers of fatigue and the effects of psychoactive substances on them. This study aimed to identify physiological biomarkers of fatigue by evaluating the PLR and VEPs. These modalities were validated against the PST, pupillary unrest index parameters, and blink-rate analysis to assess autonomic and cortical contributions to fatigue. This study examined the effects of 48-hour sleep deprivation on pupillary behavior in 18 healthy adults under controlled conditions. Analysis of PLR dynamics revealed that the dilation-phase parameters DDil1 and DDil2, corresponding to pupil diameters at 20% and 80% recovery, respectively, were sensitive to changes in autonomic activation. These complemented the established fatigue indices, including constriction velocity, relative amplitude, time of minimum diameter, and latency. Visual evoked potentials analysis demonstrated that sustained wakefulness modulated cortical responses, with a delay and amplitude reduction in the N145 component. Biomarkers from the pupillary reflex dilation phase and N145 LAT in VEP recordings serve as reliable indicators of fatigue severity, as corroborated by the PST and Stanford Sleepiness Scale assessments. papers.title: Pharmacotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of the most frequent psychiatric comorbidities in PTSD.
papers.abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is trauma- and stressor-related disorder frequently associated with somatic and psychiatric comorbidities. The most frequent psychiatric comorbidities are major depressive disorder (MDD), sleep disturbances, alcohol use disorders (AUD) and psychoses. The lack of clinical improvement is frequent in PTSD, and presence of comorbidities complicates PTSD treatment. This narrative review covered pharmacotherapy of common psychiatric comorbidities in PTSD (MDD, psychosis, sleep disturbances, especially obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and insomnia and AUD. We searched for novel data in reviews, randomized clinical trials, open labeled studies in English language through June 2026, identified using PubMed/MEDLINE/Web of Sciences/Google Scholar and clinical practice guidelines from the American Psychological Association for the Treatment of PTSD in adults (2025), and the US Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense from 2023. We discussed available evidence related to pharmacotherapy of PTSD with comorbidities. The vast majority of PTSD patients have at least one psychiatric comorbidity. Pharmacological treatment represents a challenge, given that pharmacological agents used to treat PTSD mostly do not affect symptoms of other comorbid disorders. Therefore, the choice of medications is highly individual, depending on the clinical presentation, tolerability issues, physical comorbidities, and patient preference.

papers.title: A volumetric threshold and age-dependent remodeling are associated with residual obstructive sleep apnea after adenotonsillectomy in children.
papers.abstract: Adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet residual disease persists in a notable subset of children. Traditional preoperative assessments reflect patient characteristics rather than airway anatomy, while prior cone-beam CT (CBCT) studies required extra research-only scans. We evaluated whether postoperative CBCT-measured upper-airway volume distinguishes complete OSA resolution from residual disease, and assessed age-related postoperative soft-tissue remodeling. This single-center retrospective STROBE-compliant cohort enrolled 238 children aged 3-10 years with PSG-confirmed OSA who underwent coblation adenotonsillectomy, with clinically indicated pre- and 3-month postoperative CBCT. Postoperative OAHI <1 defined complete resolution, and OAHI ≥5 defined residual OSA. ROC and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed. Mean OAHI decreased from 16.8 to 5.4 events/h (*p*<0.001). Complete resolution was achieved in 63.4% patients. The optimal postoperative airway volume cutoff was 10.5 cm³ (AUC=0.89). Postoperative volume <10.5 cm³, adenoid regrowth, high preoperative OAHI, younger age (3.0-3.9 years), and tongue-base hypertrophy were independent predictors of residual OSA. Postoperative upper-airway volume of 10.5 cm³ effectively stratifies residual OSA risk. Young age independently predicts persistent disease, likely due to incomplete soft tissue remodeling. This CBCT-based stratification uses clinically acquired imaging without extra radiation exposure.

papers.title: Prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation combined with cognitive training reduces anxiety, daytime sleepiness, and cognitive complaints in women after COVID-19: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Persistent anxiety, disturbed sleep, and subjective cognitive complaints are frequent and often co-occur after COVID-19, especially in women, yet interventions addressing them together are limited. We examined whether adding left-prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to cognitive training reduces these symptoms in women with post-COVID cognitive complaints. In a single-centre, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 30 women with confirmed prior COVID-19 and self-reported cognitive decline (Mini-Mental State Examination ≥ 24; no diagnosed neurodegenerative disorder) were allocated to three groups (n = 10 each): cognitive training plus active tDCS (CT + tDCS), cognitive training plus sham tDCS (CT + sham), or cognitive training only (CT only). Active tDCS targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (2 mA, 20 min; anode F3, return F7) across nine sessions over three weeks. Anxiety (Beck Anxiety Inventory), daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale), cognition (Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination-Revised), reaction times (psychomotor speed), and prefrontal electroencephalographic (EEG) cortical arousal and frontal asymmetry were assessed at baseline and after the ninth session; there was no follow-up. All participants completed the trial (no dropout). Groups were compared using analysis of covariance adjusted for the corresponding baseline score, with non-parametric confirmation and false-discovery-rate correction. Relative to both comparison groups, the CT + tDCS group showed significantly lower anxiety and daytime sleepiness and higher global cognition, memory, and fluency, with faster reaction times (all corrected p < .05). Cortical arousal increased and frontal asymmetry shifted toward greater relative left-frontal activation. The CT + sham and CT only groups did not differ from each other, and near-ceiling attention and visuospatial scores were unchanged. Adding left-prefrontal tDCS to cognitive training reduced anxiety and daytime sleepiness and improved cognition and psychomotor speed in women with post-COVID cognitive complaints, with parallel changes in prefrontal EEG markers. Confirmation in larger samples is needed.

papers.title: Associations of sleep duration and sleep-timing patterns with depressive mood and suicidal outcomes in Korean adolescents.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration, sleep timing, and weekday-weekend sleep-timing differences are interrelated characteristics associated with adolescent mental health. Categorizing continuous measures and interpreting mutually adjusted estimates as independent effects may obscure nonlinear patterns and their shared derivation. We examined associations of corrected mid-sleep on free days (MSFsc), weekly average sleep duration, and the absolute weekday-weekend sleep midpoint difference with depressive mood and suicidal outcomes. This cross-sectional study used data from the nationally representative 2025 Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey. Descriptive analyses included 48,426 adolescents with valid sleep-derived variables, and adjusted models included 48,416 complete cases. Survey-weighted logistic regression with restricted cubic splines evaluated nonlinear associations of the three continuous sleep descriptors with depressive mood, suicidal ideation, suicide plan, and suicide attempt. Secondary analyses examined categorical sleep-timing groups, sequential adjustment models, and exploratory combined sleep-timing group-sleep-duration profiles. Weekly average sleep duration and the absolute weekday-weekend sleep midpoint difference were associated with all four outcomes. Sleep duration was nonlinear for all outcomes, with higher odds at shorter durations. The midpoint difference was nonlinear only for depressive mood and was otherwise generally monotonic. MSFsc showed overall and nonlinear associations with depressive mood, suicidal ideation, and suicide plan, but not suicide attempt in the primary analysis (overall p = 0.054; nonlinearity p = 0.993); this result was sensitive to exclusion of extreme MSFsc values. Categorical sleep-timing group estimates changed substantially after adjustment for sleep duration and midpoint difference. In exploratory combined-profile analyses, < 5 h of sleep was associated with higher odds across all sleep-timing groups, but only 4 of 72 direct contrasts remained significant after false-discovery-rate adjustment. Very short sleep duration and larger weekday-weekend sleep midpoint differences showed the most consistent associations with depressive mood and suicidal outcomes. MSFsc associations varied across outcomes and were less robust for suicide attempt. Because the sleep descriptors share timing information, mutually adjusted estimates should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than independent causal effects. Longitudinal studies using more detailed circadian and sleep measures are needed.

papers.title: Institutional Variation in Electroencephalography Utilization in Neonates With Complex Congenital Heart Disease Across the United States and Its Association With Outcomes.
papers.abstract: Neonates with complex congenital heart disease are at increased risk for perioperative brain injury and seizures. Electroencephalography (EEG) detects clinical and subclinical seizures, but national utilization patterns remain poorly characterized. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Pediatric Health Information System (2016-2025) of neonates ≤28 days with dextro-transposition of the great arteries or single-ventricle physiology undergoing surgical repair or palliation. Mixed-effects logistic regression with hospital as a random effect identified predictors of EEG utilization. Among 13 202 neonates, 1654 (12.5%) underwent EEG monitoring. EEG monitoring was performed in only 10.8% of neonates with dextro-transposition of the great arteries, 16% of those with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and 13% of those with non- hypoplastic left heart syndrome single-ventricle lesions. EEG utilization increased from ~6% in 2016 to >14% in 2025, while seizure detection among EEG-monitored patients increased from 13% to ~26% (both P-trend<0.01). Utilization varied substantially across hospitals (0% to >40%), persisting after adjustment for surgical volume. EEG-monitored neonates had higher seizure detection (21.8% versus 5.2%), longer length of stay (33 versus 24 days), and higher hospitalization costs ($344 719 versus $174 865; all P<0.01). In multivariable analysis, EEG utilization was independently associated with seizures (OR ~4), dextro-transposition of the great arteries, and hypoplastic left heart syndrome, but not with cardiac arrest, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, or hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. EEG utilization in neonates with complex congenital heart disease is increasing but remains low and highly variable across US centers. The association of EEG use with higher mortality and costs may reflect confounding by indication or illness severity. Standardized protocols are needed to optimize neurologic monitoring and improve long-term outcomes.

papers.title: Epidemiology, Complications, and Management of Complications of Achondroplasia: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Achondroplasia is a rare genetic condition associated with considerable clinical burden. This study examined the clinical burden of achondroplasia, including epidemiology, condition complications and their management, and the estimated prevalence of common complications. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted (September 2025) to identify articles published from 2011. As a result of heterogeneity across studies, meta-analyses of complication prevalence were restricted to pediatric and adolescent populations. Overall, 200 studies were included. Forty-five studies reported epidemiological data; the prevalence of achondroplasia ranged from one to 67 per 100,000 births. The most common neurological complications were cervicomedullary compression/craniocervical junction stenosis (mean 34%; n = 13) and foramen magnum narrowing (FMN; mean 26%; n = 21). The top respiratory complications were sleep disordered breathing (SDB; mean 60%; n = 13) and obstructive sleep apnea (mean 48%; n = 27). Ear, nose, and throat (ENT) complications comprised ear infections (mean 40%; n = 12) and hearing impairment (mean 40%; n = 16). Common orthopedic complications included kyphosis (mean 43%; n = 22) and bowing of legs or genu varum (mean 39%; n = 7). The top complications among pediatric populations were SDB (mean 65% [95% confidence interval (CI) 36, 85]; n = 13) and FMN (mean 56% [37, 73]; n = 20). Cervicomedullary decompression (mean 11%; n = 22) was a more frequent treatment option for neurologic complications than suboccipital decompression (mean 19%; n = 3). Typical interventions included ENT procedures (mean 40%; n = 37) and surgery for orthopedic complications (mean 28%; n = 27). Twenty-six studies reported complications from limb-lengthening surgeries (mean age of treatment 6.2-16.9 years). This SLR and meta-analysis underscore the significant clinical burden related to complications and their management in individuals with achondroplasia. Prevalence estimates varied widely by geography, reflecting differences in data sources, case ascertainment, and reporting practices. The high frequency and severity of complications underscore the need for effective treatments to reduce complication burden and improve patient quality of life.

papers.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation in perioperative neurocognitive disorders: clinical evidence and mechanistic perspectives.
papers.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) are common neurological complications in older surgical patients and are associated with impaired recovery, loss of independence, and worse quality of life. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a non-invasive neuromodulatory intervention with plausible effects on inflammatory, autonomic, sleep, pain, and cognitive-network pathways. We conducted a PROSPERO-registered systematic review of direct perioperative randomized clinical evidence and, when outcomes were sufficiently comparable, an exploratory meta-analysis. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 5 August 2026. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. Mechanistic and translational evidence was synthesized separately using a structured narrative approach. Four randomized trials enrolled or randomized 480 participants, of whom 469 contributed to reported analyses. Two trials involving 220 participants assessed related but non-identical early postoperative cognitive-decline constructs: one used dNCR and the other investigator-defined traditional POCD. Both studies individually favored taVNS, and the individual study estimates were treated as the primary evidence. A post hoc exploratory cross-construct synthesis yielded an RR of 0.34 (95% CI 0.18-0.64). Because the contributing trials used non-equivalent cognitive definitions, stimulation regimens, and comparator conditions, this secondary pooled estimate should not be interpreted as representing either a single standardized cognitive outcome or the effect of a single standardized taVNS intervention. A separate multicenter trial reported postoperative delirium in 12.0% versus 25.3% of participants (risk ratio 0.47, 95% confidence interval 0.23-0.98), and another trial showed more favorable postoperative Montreal Cognitive Assessment trajectories. Beyond clinical outcomes, the broader mechanistic literature supports a multilevel neurophysiological rationale for taVNS, consistent with possible modulation of auricular vagal afferent-nucleus tractus solitarius signaling, locus coeruleus and autonomic regulation, inflammatory reflex pathways, splenic sympathetic-cholinergic immune modulation, blood-brain barrier/neurovascular unit protection, glial responses, sleep-arousal regulation, and cognitive-network plasticity. However, most mechanistic evidence remains derived from preclinical or non-perioperative studies, and no causal pathway linking target engagement to cognitive improvement has been established. Current evidence suggests a promising but preliminary clinical signal for taVNS in perioperative neurocognitive disorders. However, certainty remains low to very low, and routine clinical implementation is not yet supported. Available adverse-event data are insufficient to establish perioperative safety or to exclude uncommon cardiovascular or autonomic adverse events. Standardized PND outcomes, credible sham conditions, optimized stimulation dose and timing, systematic adverse-event ascertainment, multimodal target-engagement biomarkers, and risk-enriched confirmatory trials are priorities for future development. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261468039, Identifier: CRD420261468039.

papers.title: Sleep duration and risk of post-stroke depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

However, the relationship between sleep duration and the risk of post-stroke depression remains controversial. To investigate the association between sleep duration and the risk of post-stroke depression. Relevant studies investigating the association between sleep duration and post-stroke depression were searched in five English databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL) and four Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, and China Biology Medicine Database) from inception to January 2026. Data extraction and quality assessment of the included literature were independently performed by two investigators. Meta-analyses were conducted using Stata 16.0 software. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using either a fixed-effects or a random-effects model. The analysis included 6 articles, encompassing a total of 5,624 cases. Meta-analysis showed that short sleep duration was associated with an increased risk of post-stroke depression [OR = 1.93, 95% CI(1.56-2.38), p < 0.05], whereas long sleep duration was not significantly associated with the risk [OR = 1.29, 95% CI(1.00-1.66), p > 0.05]. papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea and long COVID syndrome: a scoping review of current evidence in adults.
papers.abstract: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is a prevalent sleep disorder characterized by intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation, contributing to systemic inflammation and autonomic dysfunction. Long COVID refers to persistent symptoms following acute COVID-19 infection. Emerging evidence suggests an association between OSA and persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms, potentially mediated by overlapping biological pathways; however, the direction and causality of this relationship remain uncertain. This scoping review aimed to examine the current evidence regarding the different associations between OSA and Long COVID in adults, summarize the reported clinical findings, and explore the proposed pathophysiological mechanisms linking OSA and Long COVID. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for studies published between 2020 and 2026. Eligible studies included observational studies, clinical trials, and reviews involving adults with OSAand/or Long COVID syndrome. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and synthesized findings thematically. Of 184 identified records, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria. Evidence suggested different associations between OSA and Long COVID across the included studies. Proposed mechanisms included intermittent hypoxia, systemic inflammation, autonomic dysregulation, sleep fragmentation, and circadian disturbance; however, these mechanisms were not consistently measured across studies. Reported Long COVID manifestations among patients with OSA included fatigue, respiratory impairment, cognitive dysfunction, and cardiovascular complications. Evidence regarding the impact of OSA treatment on Long COVID outcomes was limited. Current evidence suggests an association between OSA and Long COVID, although the nature and direction of this association vary across studies. However, the evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Further longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relationship and determine whether effective OSA management can improve Long COVID outcomes.

papers.title: Associations of rotating shift work with depressive symptoms among Chinese nurses: exploratory indirect associations through sleep problems.
papers.abstract: Rotating shift work has been associated with depressive symptoms, but its association with depressive symptom severity and the statistical intermediary pattern involving sleep quality remain incompletely understood. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of baseline data (2021-2024) from the Chinese Nurses' Health Cohort Study (TARGET), including 43,697 registered nurses from 105 hospitals across 15 provinces in China. Primary analyses compared rotating shifts with fixed day shifts, while fixed night shifts were included in sensitivity analyses. Depressive symptoms and sleep quality were assessed using the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Multivariable ordinal and binary logistic regression models were used to estimate associations. Exploratory model-based indirect associations were estimated using probit models with bootstrap resampling. Among the participants, 93.8% were women and 64.4% worked rotating shifts. Compared with fixed day shifts, rotating shifts were consistently associated with higher odds of depressive symptoms across four cumulative PHQ-9 contrasts (OR range, 1.471-1.500; all P < 0.001) and with poor sleep quality (OR, 1.592; 95% CI, 1.514-1.674; P < 0.001). Poor sleep quality statistically accounted for 38.6% (95% CI, 34.2%-43.2%) of the observed association between rotating shifts and depressive symptoms under the fitted model. All seven PSQI components showed statistically supported indirect associations. Sleep latency had the numerically largest estimated percentage statistically accounted for (39.3%; 95% CI, 24.2%-45.0%). In the reverse-pathway specification, depressive symptoms statistically accounted for 14.8% (95% CI, 13.7%-16.0%) of the observed association between rotating shifts and poor sleep quality. Rotating shifts were consistently associated with greater depressive symptom severity and poor sleep quality. The observed statistical intermediary patterns highlight sleep quality, particularly sleep latency, as an important priority for assessment and for prospective evaluation of sleep-focused strategies among nurses working rotating shifts. Although causal direction cannot be established from these cross-sectional data, the findings provide a focused basis for future longitudinal and interventional research. papers.title: Reconsidering early Parkinson's disease: dopaminergic hyperactivation as a pre-degenerative functional stage.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurological condition primarily caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc). However, recent research suggests a functional hyperactivity phase that precedes neuronal degeneration and may hold therapeutic potential. This study was conducted as a narrative review to synthesize evidence on early-phase dopaminergic hyperactivation in PD and different interventions that could potentially delay the onset of PD. We identified various toxins and genetic mutations that increase neuronal excitability, which eventually progresses to depletion of SNc neurons. This disrupts the circuitry of the basal ganglia, resulting in compensatory hyperactivity and increased dopamine release. Preclinical, neuroimaging, genetic, and clinical evidence supports that neurodegeneration in PD is preceded by a period of neuronal hyperactivation marked by increased glutamatergic transmission, calcium dysregulation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, revealing altered striatal connections and increased dopamine turnover. This hyperdopaminergic disorder manifests clinically as early non-motor symptoms like autonomic dysfunction, REM sleep behavior disorder, and hyposmia. Multimodal biomarkers that combine genetic, imaging, and electrophysiological data can detect this pre-degenerative stage, making early intervention possible. Calcium channel modulators, mitochondrial stabilizers, metabolic regulators, and anti-inflammatory medications that target the NRF2 and PPAR-γ pathways are examples of novel strategies for preserving neuronal integrity. Therefore, redefining PD as a disorder of reversible neuronal stress instead of permanent degeneration can lead to opportunities for both early and long-term neuroprotection.

papers.title: Nogo-related frontal theta-band activity after magnetic seizure therapy in treatment-resistant depression: an exploratory task-based EEG study.
papers.abstract: Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) is an emerging convulsive treatment for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) with efficacy comparable to electroconvulsive therapy and superior cognitive safety. However, its neurophysiological mechanisms-particularly those underlying conflict monitoring and response inhibition-remain unclear. Frontal midline theta-band activity indexes anterior cingulate-prefrontal cognitive-control activity and may reflect inefficient neural processing in depression. In this open-label, single-arm trial, 19 patients with TRD (16 female; mean age 20.89 ± 8.16 years; 10 of the 19 participants were minors) received 6-12 MST sessions using 100-Hz double-cone coil stimulation targeting bilateral F3/F4 frontal regions. Clinical assessments, including the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24), Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), and 64-channel Go/Nogo task-based electroencephalography (EEG), were performed before and after treatment. EEG outcome measures included event-related potentials (N2/P3), time-frequency power (theta/beta), microstate dynamics, and theta-beta cross-frequency coupling. Following MST, patients showed significant reductions in depressive symptoms (HAMD: 40.53 ± 10.25 to 22.53 ± 11.21; MADRS: 35.68 ± 8.84 to 20.68 ± 11.12). Response rates ranged from 42.1% to 57.9%. Behavioral data could not be formally analyzed due to incomplete data storage. At an uncorrected threshold, total Nogo-related theta-band activity (4-7 Hz) at Fz and FCz was lower after treatment; however, these effects did not survive FDR correction. ERP amplitudes did not change significantly. Exploratory microstate analysis showed nominal changes in Map4 AUC during Go processing and Map2 duration during Nogo processing; none survived FDR correction. These parameters should not be interpreted as reflecting changes in neural activation or inhibitory preparation. No significant changes were observed in theta-beta cross-frequency coupling or Go-condition theta power. These preliminary findings suggest that MST was associated with short-term symptom improvement and lower total Nogo-related theta-band activity at an uncorrected threshold. Because no control group, complete behavioral data, normative comparison, Time × Condition interaction, or EEG-clinical association was available, these findings cannot establish causal mechanisms, condition specificity, improved neural efficiency, or biomarker utility. Replication in adequately powered controlled studies with complete behavioral and longitudinal clinical measures is required.

papers.title: Sleep and circadian disruption as systemic drivers of breast cancer metastasis: A tri-pathway mechanistic model.
papers.abstract: Sleep deficiency and circadian disruption are emerging modifiable risk factors in breast cancer. However, their specific role in driving metastasis remains incompletely defined. This review maps circadian disturbance to metastatic competence through three convergent systemic pathways. First is neuroendocrine disruption via melatonin suppression. Second is immunological dysregulation characterized by chronic inflammation and myeloid derived suppressor cell expansion. Third is metabolic reprogramming involving insulin resistance and altered adipokine signaling. These converging signals lower critical barriers at every step of metastasis. They promote epithelial mesenchymal transition and local invasion. They support circulating tumor cell survival. They enable pre metastatic niche formation. They also trigger reactivation of dormant micrometastases. We evaluate clinical biomarkers of circadian disruption including cortisol rhythms, urinary melatonin, and actigraphy. We link these sleep metrics to patient outcomes. We also discuss therapeutic opportunities such as melatonin supplementation, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, and personalized chrono chemotherapy. By establishing circadian health as an actionable axis in metastasis prevention, this review provides a framework for integrating chronobiology into breast cancer management and survivorship care.

papers.title: Integrative therapies for symptom management in dementia from a palliative perspective: narrative review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
papers.abstract: Dementia affects over 55 million people worldwide, with behavioral and psychological symptoms (BPSD) impacting over 90% of individuals. Conventional pharmacotherapies offer limited benefits with substantial side effects. Integrative care therapies (ICT) represent a complementary approach, yet the evidence supporting their use has been largely absent from the palliative care literature. This narrative review synthesizes ICT systematic reviews and meta-analyses to bridge this gap. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between 2015 and June 2026 evaluating ICT for dementia symptom management. Seminal earlier works were also included when updated reviews were unavailable. Individual randomized controlled trials (RCTs), validation studies, and non-English publications were excluded, except selected sources cited for mechanistic, safety, regulatory, or pivotal-trial context. Cognitive stimulation achieved the highest evidence certainty, with high-certainty evidence for communication and social interaction and moderate-certainty evidence for cognition, quality of life (QOL), and challenging behaviors. Music therapy showed moderate-certainty evidence for depression improvement but not agitation. Light therapy and movement-based mind-body therapies (MBT) demonstrated benefit across the broadest range of domains-including cognition, BPSD, and sleep-though certainty remained low-to-very-low. Massage and aromatherapy showed consistent short-term benefits for agitation and depression. Acupuncture augmented conventional medication for improvement in cognition and activities of daily living (ADL). Dietary and herbal therapies contributed primarily to cognitive domains, with Ginkgo biloba showing the most robust BPSD evidence. Cannabinoids showed preliminary evidence for agitation and in severe disease. Across modalities, effects were often limited to the treatment period, early-stage disease showed the most robust benefits, and safety profiles were favorable. Only cognitive stimulation and music therapy achieved moderate or higher Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) ratings. Multiple ICT modalities show promising evidence for dementia symptom management that aligns with palliative care principles, though most evidence is of low-to-very-low certainty. Future research should prioritize pragmatic trials in hospice and palliative care settings using outcomes meaningful to this context, including comfort, caregiver experience, and healthcare utilization.

papers.title: The interplay of exercise, immunity, and suboptimal health in college students: an integrative narrative review with public health implications.
papers.abstract: The immune system, vital for pathogen defense and tissue repair, is strongly influenced by lifestyle. With declining physical activity and rising chronic disease burdens, the role of exercise in modulating immunity has drawn growing attention. College students, undergoing critical life transitions, are susceptible to lifestyle-related risks such as sedentary behavior, insufficient sleep, and high psychological stress, which often lead to suboptimal health status. Immune and inflammatory risks are a concern among college students: prolonged sedentary behavior, chronic sleep deprivation, and elevated psychological stress frequently co-occur. Each of these behaviors is associated with low-grade inflammation and altered immune regulation in adults, and their clustering in students is therefore a reasonable basis for concern, although the strength of the association with immune outcomes has seldom been measured directly in this group. The term suboptimal health status is used in this review as a self-reported functional syndrome, defined in Section 3.4, rather than as an established clinical entity. We examine the effects of different physical activities on immune function, chronic low-grade inflammation, and suboptimal health status in college students, outlining the basic framework of exercise immunology and distinguishing acute from chronic exercise responses. Evidence is categorized by exercise type, including moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, high-intensity training, resistance training, and mind-body practices, and their mechanisms, such as myokine-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling, immune cell mobilization, fat loss, and the mediation of sleep and emotion, are summarized. We critically discuss the methodological challenges in this field, separating two sources of disagreement that are often conflated: study design, which determines the causal question a study can answer, and measurement method, which determines how accurately exposure and outcome are captured. We analyze the limitations of each, including the inability of cross-sectional studies to establish causality, measurement bias in self-reported data, and ecological validity and compliance issues in trials, and we note how the same distinction applies to outcome assessment, from self-reported symptoms to immune-cell, cytokine, and clinical infection measures. Notable gaps are identified, including the "population mismatch" whereby findings from other populations are extrapolated to college students, limitations in sample selection and measurement standardization, and the lack of individualized and comprehensive intervention studies. This narrative review underscores the importance of understanding the relationship between exercise and immunity in college students, provides an overview of current knowledge, identifies critical limitations, and proposes future directions. Evidence was assembled through a structured narrative search, and findings obtained directly in college students are distinguished throughout from those extrapolated from athletic or clinical populations. It also offers public health implications for Chinese university settings, emphasizing targeted health education, campus-wide exercise interventions, sedentary behavior reduction, and integrated sleep and stress management to promote student wellbeing.
